results.title: How to design CI/CD pipelines. In 2010 when Continuous Delivery was… | by Pat Conheady | Cognizant Servian
results.content: # How to design CI/CD pipelines. Today your organisation is more likely to already have ‘CI/CD pipelines’ but find that they are not fit for purpose — for example, the release cycle requires multiple pipelines to be run in ‘just’ the right order, with the right variables set by hand, etc. Therefore there is a need to put some structure around the process of designing CI/CD pipelines, which this article will set out. The term ‘CI/CD pipeline’ is a much-abused phrase which really just means some automation that helps you build, test and deploy your code (regardless of whether you’re actually doing CI and/or CD). ## Design process for a pipeline. Every pipeline is different (somehow!) but I find that the design process involves much the same steps each time. ### Step 1: Requirements gathering for the pipeline. * When triggered by a commit, be clear about which branches should be considered and whether there are any other conditions, e.g. only run the pipeline if certain paths were changed since the last pipeline run. ### Step 2: Sketch the pipeline as a diagram. Note that approval gates should be driven by requirements collected in step 1, not added just because they seem like ‘good practice’ for a pipeline. By the time you get to step 5 below (design review), it might have some more details, e.g.:. For any of the steps that don’t already have off-the-shelf implementations, you need to write custom code. ### Step 6: Implement the pipeline. Note that while implementing the pipeline, it is best to avoid repeatedly running the pipeline to troubleshoot issues, particularly the behaviour of custom code. You should understand your agent’s configuration and environment well enough to simply run each step outside of the pipeline until it works. ### Step 7: Put the pipeline into production. Take care not to have conflicting outputs e.g. one pipeline overwrites the other pipeline’s build artifact. * time taken for pipeline to run — e.g. impact on Developer Experience and lead time from code to release;. * the balance between pre-provisioning tools and data (e.g. base images) onto agents, versus installing them during each pipeline run.

In this blog, we will deeply examine the specific touchpoints where AI code generators can be embedded into CI/CD workflows, the technical patterns and tools that enable such integrations, and how to implement them in production-grade environments while maintaining high confidence, reproducibility, and auditability. The blog is written with the intent to assist experienced developers, DevOps engineers, and platform teams in understanding the architectural strategies and operational best practices for embedding AI-driven code generation inside CI/CD pipelines. ##### **Why Developers Should Use AI Code Generators in CI/CD Pipelines**. AI can augment the developer’s productivity by suggesting boilerplate code, generating missing test cases, updating configuration files, or even fixing simple bugs automatically based on the context of recent changes. ##### **Main Integration Points for AI Code Generators in CI/CD Pipelines**.
